subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
One of the professed policies of this administration is the development of inter-empire trade, and with that policy, generally speaking, the Conservative party is in hearty accord provided always-and I want to emphasize this proviso-that such a policy does not involve the sacrifice of any basic industry in this country, such as has happened as a result of the Australian treaty and its effect on our dairy industry. But in the light of this declared policy, what is to be thought of the recent declaration of Sir Richard Squires, Premier of Newfoundland, who recently visited this country, and who in a newspaper interview is reported to have said, in effect, that he found Canada cold to any proposals for closer trade relations? What underlies this statement? A declaration from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) would seem .to be in order. Newfoundland is one of the oldest British colonies, and is one of our nearest neighbours. We have a large trade with that colony now. There is no reason why we should not have it all. But Sir Richard Squires went to the south of us and got a cordial reception, and before we know it he will have negotiated a trade treaty with the United States that will be altogether to the detriment of Canada, as happened once before.
Connected closely with this question of inter-empire trade is the question of trade generally with the countries of the West Indies and central and south America. I had the good fortune to visit thirteen West Indian and central and south American ports during the month of'January last. Primarily the trip was a holiday, but I had the good fortune to have with me letters of introduction to the

The Budget-Mr. Hanson

various managers, inspectors and supervisors of the Royal Bank of Canada, that great Canadian financial institution which has such extensive ramifications in all those countries. Being keenly interested in the development of trade with these countries, especially as such development may tend to the betterment of the welfare of the maritime provinces, I sought and obtained a great deal of valuable information.
I do not venture to go into any detail in regard to this important subject-time will not permit-but I have one constructive suggestion to make. With the Latin-American countries there is an abundant opportunity to conduct a large and profitable trade, most of which to-day is going to the United States. I found that business men in these Latin-American nations cordially detest the United States and would be delighted to open up new trade channels with Canada, but there is no point of contact save and except through the medium of the bank.
I was told that what is required at the moment are some live trade commissioners who have a competent knowledge of the Spanish language, I commend that suggestion to the minister. That is what the banks do; as far as possible, they train these men before they go there, and on their arrival they rapidly learn the language and become a valuable asset to the banks. I met Mr. Young, our trade commissioner at Port of Spain, Trinidad. I have no doubt that he is doing a good work there, but if one has visited that part of the world one will realize how great are the distances between the various ports and islands and how difficult is communication. Intercommunication between these ports and islands is very slow. Transportation converges on New York or Canada, and one man cannot possibly cover the whole territory. I suggest therefore the appointment of a competent itrade commissioner at Panama, which is the pivotal point and now the most important port on the great highway from North America to South America. Advantage should be taken of the ramifications of the Canadian banks which are located at all these important points. They are willing, indeed eager, to assist in the creation of Canadian trade in this region and I commend this suggestion to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Like my friend the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), I have a suggestion to make to the government, which is this: In view of the impending special session of the United States congress called to meet on the
17t'h of April and the certainty almost of further tariff changes sure to affect adversely Canadian trade with the United States, I suggest to the government, and to the Finance minister especially that this budget be not closed-I do not mean to keep the debate open; God forbid, but I suggest that it is possible to devise some means Whereby, after the tariff proposals presented to congress in special session have become known, this parliament at this session may be prepared to take yand do take, action to protect our position. If you let it go a year it will be too late. That is my word to the Minister of Finance.
I have had large dealings, covering many years, with United States business men, and I find them among the keenest and most honourable business men in the world. At the same time they are hard bargainers, but they respect always the Canadian business man who stands up for his rights and who meets them squarely and on equal terms.	I fear
that the same cannot be said for the average United States politician, but I have no doubt that if this country meets the situation about to be created, resolutely, firmly and with a determination to protect Canadian interests, we shall at once-obtain the respect of that nation and bring them to a realization of the fact-and they are already realizing it, if one is to believe what was written only a day or two ago in the Wall Street Journal and New York Evening Post-that they cannot afford to alienate trade with their best customer. I say therefore to the Finance minister that he should not close the budget proposals, and that if necessary this house should be adjourned, if other business is not available, and reassemble with the idea of dealing frankly and adequately with the situation that is bound to be presented. The Canadian people will expect any government charged with administration of our affairs to meet this situation resolutely and courageously, and if this government does not do it the frowning disapproval of the Canadian people will be manifested immediately and a new government, prepared to face the situation courageously by and through the means that are easily available, will carry out the will of the Canadian people.
What is there in the budget proposals of 1929 which makes provision for reasonable safeguarding and protection of the interest of this country, either agricultural or industrial? Absolutely nothing, and at a time, if ever there was a time when the agricultural and industrial interests, the interests of employer as

The Budget-Mr. McMillan

well as of employee, should be safeguarded and protected. This party to which I have the honour to belong is therefore amply justified in bringing forward such an amendment *to the budget as has been proposed by the hon. member for South Wellington and I heartily give my assent thereto.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the attention of the house for a few moments this evening? Notwithstanding all that has been said by hon. members opposite, I consider this country fortunate in having as its Minister of Finance a gentleman of the calibre of Hon. James Robb. The budget which he presented on March 1 is a model of precision; 1 congratulate him on its presentation. It's substance should gladden the heart of every Canadian. It is most encouraging to think that after meeting all our obligations, in six years Canada has been able to reduce her national debt by over 8226,000,000.
The vision of the Minister of Finance enables him to view this country as a great estate, a goodly heritage in the form of a big farm, placed in his charge under a heavy mortgage resulting from the war, and after being exploited by those who seemed willing to do almost anything to retain power and position. Like a thrifty parent with the lasting welfare of a large family at heart he realizes the wisdom of paying off the mortgage before dividing his property. His family is large; their names are agriculture, forests, mines, fisheries and numerous additional secondary births many of which have grown great and vigorous through the support of the eldest son, agriculture, but which persists in asking further nourishment from the same source. This eldest son, agriculture, has been a most dutiful and industrious child; he has toiled and spun; he has sacrificed and given of his substance for the whole family, and no one knows this better than the Minister of Finance. If it were not for the continued stamina of this eldest son the whole family fabric would fall to pieces. But there is some indefinable thing called high protection standing in the way, placed there by a group of trustees into whose keeping the property was confided some years ago, with disastrous results. This doctrine of protection somewhat blurs the vision of the minister and prevents him from seeing as clearly as he might. His 
eldest son, agriculture, is continually endeavouring to appeal to his reason, tr3ring to make him see a little more clearly, but the blur still continues. In that respect his senior partner, the Prime Minister, has no misgivings; his vision is as clear as the noon-day sun. He knows what should be done, but he also realizes that it is not what any great statesman thinks ought to be done, that it is not always wise to attempt at the moment, but rather what step in advance can be taken and carry your countrymen with you.
There is a further difficulty in the way; the same party which fastened that vicious principle upon the economic life of this country is still lurking around the corner always ready to raise the tariff as high as Haman's gallows, as they did on July 13, 1926, the very moment they were sworn in. Moreover, that party now has at its head a brilliant and astute leader whom I greatly admire and whose political ebullitions throughout Canada last year require some consideration. I admire his amazing energy and the spirit with which he endeavours to revive a protective policy which has been rejected by the people of Canada no less than seven times since the beginning of 1896-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And which is still in
force.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and which was given such a cold shoulder at the Winnipeg convention that they were afraid even to mention the name "protectionist," and where their resolution on trade policies was an emasculated expression disavowing the very name of protection. After having taken such an attitude, and more particularly after their milk and water amendment to the budget last year, why do they not come out boldly and repudiate the whole system? If they would only do that they would be on solid ground and might attain some healthy growth, but instead the old protectionist horse is trotted out once more. It came into sight very clearly the other day, with the leader of the opposition holding a string around its neck and his leading lieutenant hanging on by the tail.
Immediately after the close of last session the leader of the opposition went to Toronto and told his Tory stalwarts that the King government were imposing such a burden of taxation on this country and were so utterly extravagant, particularly with respect to undertakings designed to please their friends, that nothing but an aroused public opinion would remedy the situation. If only he had told his supporters that the King government

The Budget-Mr. McMillan
were standing like watch-dogs guarding the public treasury against the attempted raids of himself and his friends it would have been nearer the facts. Every member of this house knows that when we were considering t'he estimates last year, hon. gentlemen opposite were always asking for increased expenditures; during the course of one day no less than seventeen hon. gentlemen opposite demanded increased expenditures, while just the other day they were highly indignant because this government would not immediately embark on a highway policy which would lead to the expenditure of $200,000,000 or more.
It is well known that the Department of Public Works is necessarily one of the great spending departments of the government; this is due to the necessary expenditure of money on dredging and other works to provide further canal and harbour accommodation and also to the construction of public buildings and other requirements brought about by the increasing needs of a young and growing country. The expenditure upon public works should bear some relationship to the growing trade of the country. During the fiscal year ending March 31, 1914, when our Conservative friends were in power, the foreign trade of Canada amounted to $1,074,000,000, and $27,991,000, or 2.7 per cent of the total foreign trade, was expended upon public works. During the last fiscal year, when the foreign trade of Canada had increased to over $2,359,000,000, this government expended upon public works, not $27,991,000 as their opponents had done, but only $17,408,000, or less than three-quarters of one per cent of the foreign trade of Canada as against 2.7 per cent under Tory rule. That is a striking instance of the manner in which this government is husbanding its revenues and exercising the strictest economy consistent with efficiency in control in one of the great departments of the public service of Canada.
After the hon. leader of the Conservative party left Toronto he went down to Quebec and the maritimes to enlighten the people in that part of the country. At Knowlton, Quebec, he exhorted the good women of that province to study politics, and then he proceeded to say:
Who is there that does not believe that if we had reciprocity -with the American people we would have long ago have lost our identity and been absorbed in and by the United States?
I wondered if he had lost all his common sense when he made an unguarded statement of this kind in a province where absorption with the American people would mean the loss of their long-cherished official language. But he
proceeded to say it was a shame that the home markets of the farmers of Canada had been taken away from them and given to the farmers of New Zealand and the United States. As a Canadian, Mr. Speaker, it is humiliating to me to think that the leader of a great political party would hand out such mental trash to intelligent Canadians. Does he not know that the Liberal trade policy of gradually reducing tariff restrictions upon all necessaries, together with reciprocal trade, not only with our neighbours but with the whole world, are the two factors which will tend to build up a permanently successful agriculture and encourage industry, shipping and international trade? Does he not know that Canadians have become world citizens? Does he not know that Canada has emerged from doing business on the back streets and has opened her stand upon the great international business highways of the world? Canada can no longer continue to live within herself. The manufacturer in this country who within the next five or ten years, if a Liberal government is in power, does not realize that he must cater to the world's trade, will be a back number.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They will not be in that long.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
With fewer than 10,000.000 people we now stand fifth among the great commercial nations. Our increase in international trade since 1913, and more particularly since 1921, is simply marvellous. Our per capita trade is more than double that of most countries. Situated in such a pivotal position between the orient and Australia and New Zealand on the one hand, and the old world markets on the other, with two highly equipped lines of transcontinental railway, with such a wealth of still largely undeveloped natural resources, and the highest quality of production, our watchword ought to be to scale down gradually our needless trade barriers and go forth to win in open competition with the world. We are competing successfully with the world to-day and there is no good reason why we cannot continue to fortify and improve our present favourable trade position. As Sir George Paish, the British economist, has said:
Unless the United States and many other nations cease telling their people to sell here but don't sell there, the world will, sooner or later, suffer an economic cataclysm which no country will escape.
If we are to be worthy of fully appreciating our great possibilities it is our duty to scale down gradually all needless trade bar-
The Budget-Mr. McMillan

riers and let Canada lead the way. Hon. gentlemen opposite would have this country again go through the humilitating experience it suffered between 1878 and 1896 under the national policy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You have that yet.
Mr. MeMILLAN: That policy inaugurated eighteen years of stagnation in Canada, with trade dead, debt increasing, population at a standstill, immigration reduced to a minimum and migration at full flood, the greatest period of migration from Canada, more particularly to the United States. It was the dreary, hopeless period of Canadian history. During the eighteen years in which that policy strangled Canadian development, our total exports increased from $79,154,678 to $116,314,543. During the single month of July, 1927, our exports totalled $80,770,925, and in the month of July, 1928, the total was $127,368,623. The increase of July, 1928, over July, 1927, was more than $9,000,000 greater than the entire increase in exports during the whole eighteen years under the national policy. The paralyzing influence of those eighteen years of high protection in Canada should never be forgotten. Canada has never yet shaken herself entirely free from the blighting effect of that policy, and I urge upon this government that its duty is to proceed more rapidly along the lines of a well-considered tariff reduction. The danger cry has always been: Oh, we need the revenue; we must be careful. That argument can no longer be used. Every successive tariff reduction has verified our opinion in that it has yielded a greater revenue. I urge them again that we can do this kind of thing only in periods of good times. We cannot do it in times of adversity. Now is the golden opportunity and we should be taking advantage of it. Apparently, however, they seem inclined to mark time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is this the time?
Mr. MeMILLAN: It may be wise. I do not know what the special session of the United States congress will do; I am no prophet, but I know President Hoover has never shown himself to be a foolish man. There is no doubt he has a most friendly feeling towards his northern neighbour. He knows Canada is his best customer. He knows, further, Canada has a standing offer to his government of reciprocal trade in food products. He knows that 66 per cent of the United States people live in incorporated towns and cities and desire a lower cost of living. In our own particular lines Canada produces the finest quality of foodstuffs in the world. He also knows there is

a decided shortage of fresh meat products for the domestic requirements of his own country. In 1927 there was a deficiency of more than 400,000,000 pounds below the previous year's production and in 1928 there was a further deficiency of some 642,000,000 pounds. Canada is the only country from which the United States can secure a supply of disease-free, high-class fresh meat. He knows further from the lips of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King), in a declaration made openly on the floor of the house, that if Canada receives fair treatment she is open and aboveboard and willing to cooperate in every legitimate way, in so far as federal jurisdiction will permit, in the development of the St. Lawrence waterways towards which he himself has set his heart. In the face of all those facts does anyone believe that the very first international act of President Hoover will be to hand out a serious economic handicap to both his own country and Canada? I refuse to believe it; I believe the United States people have elected to the presidential chair a great American who will prove himself worthy of the name. But I deprecate the attitude of hon. gentlemen on the floor of the house towards the United States people and government. That attitude in both gesture and expression manifested at this time for purely partisan purposes i-beneath the dignity which should characterize the proceedings of this deliberative assembly. After repeated assertions by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) listen to the following:
But, I repeat, President Hoover has recently announced a policy of increasing the United States tariff against our farmers.
I dispute the imputation and I invite the hon. gentleman to quote from President Hoover's inaugural message one syllable which will bear any such construction. Mark the different tone of President Hoover's words in regard to the tariff:
Limited changes cannot, in justice to our farmers, our labour and our manufacturers, be postponed.
listen also to his noble expression in regard to permanent peace.

speechtext:
Why not ?
Mr. MeMILLAN: Bear yourself in silence. When the hon. gentleman speaks, we will listen to him. The fact is that when hon. gentlemen opposite rise to speak in parliament,

The Budget-Mr. McMillan
it is very seldom they have anything worth saying. Listen to the noble expression of President Hoover respecting permanent peace:
The United States fully accepts the profound truth that our own progress, prosperity and peace, are interlocked with the progress, prosperity and peace of all humanity. ... It is impossible my countrymen, to speak of peace without profound emotion. In thousands of homes in America, in millions of homes around the world, there are vacant chairs. It would be a shameful confession of our unworthiness if it should develop that we have abandoned the hope for which all men died. Surely civilization is old enough, surely mankind is mature enough so that we ought in our lifetime to find a way to permanent peace.
Contrast these words with the blustering, defiant mood in which the hon. member for Fort William jumps on to a big "if":
If at that special session called by President Hoover any more restrictions are placed upon our sales to the United States. . . . then we in turn should deal in a red-blooded Canadian manner with their tariff attitude towards us.
But even that does not satisfy him and he becomes still more violently bombastic, and proceeds:
I think we have been taking too white-blooded an attitude towards the United States all the time, and I submit that it is time for us to stand up and take a good red-blooded Canadian attitude.
That is the blood that courses through the veins of my hon. friend from Fort William, and it is also the blood which coursed through the veins of every member of the "shadow" cabinet when, in June 1926, they sat on the treasury benches, when the present Prime Minister metaphorically speaking, laid every one of them over his knee, and, after administering a sound spanking compelled every one of them to admit that not one of them had taken the oath of office and that they were guilty of endeavouring to mislead and deceive parliament and to put over the most indefensible act of power usurpation ever attempted on the floor of the Canadian parliament.
But that is not the spirit in which Canada should maintain the proud position which she occupies throughout the world to-day. Canada has achieved a high position in the minds and hearts of European nations. Great benefit has accrued to her through the sojourn of the Prime Minister in Great Britain and on the continent during the past year. His timely message of international peace, goodwill and conciliation rather than armaments as a means of settling disputes has lifted Canada to a high place among the nations of the world. Do these hon. gentlemen opposite want to discredit our
proud position and trail it in the dust? Canada has no<w signally qualified as interpreter nation along the lines of peace, as a means of settling international disputes. The peace of the world depends more upon establishing good relationship between the United States and Great Britain and between Great Britain and France than upon any other single factor. The people of Canada, largely made up of two dominant races-the French and the British- have learned by experience to respect and honour the respective characteristics of those races. We have long since blended together those traits of character which enable us to work hand in hand and with the heartiest feelings of kindly cooperation have enthusiastically set ourselves to the task of building up a great and prosperous nation on the northern half of the American continent; building it upon the noblest principle of humanity, namely, the principle of peace on earth and good will towards men.
With such a prospect in view, and living alongside a nation with whom we enjoy the most friendly and intimate relationship, this Dominion understands and can interpret the French, the British and the United States characteristics. We are, therefore, qualified to act as an interpreter nation, and Canada holds it in her power to cement closer and closer those bonds which exist between us. But we also hold it in our power, by just such expressions as I have indicated coming from the opposite side of this house, to blast our good reputation and discredit Canada's prestige throughout the world.
Hon. gentlemen opposite would convey the impression that the Australian trade treaty has been an injury to the Canadian dairy industry. I am not going into an elaborate analysis of the effect of that agreement, but the fact is that it has not been detrimental to the dairy interests of Canada. Every economic student of those conditions knows that until very recently Great Britain has been the world's best market for dairy products and consquently the greatest distributing and price-regulating market of the world. But what happened? On October 1, 1925, the Australian treaty came into operation. From that time on there was a steady advance in the price of butter in Canada till March of 1926 when No. 1 pasteurized butter was ten cents per pound higher in Montreal than the price of Australian butter in London, and, generally, it has remained higher ever since. During the whole of the year 1926, the averag-price of No. 1 pasteurized butter in Montreal was 2.46 cents per pound higher than Australian butter in London. For the whole year
The Budget-Mr. McMillan

1927, it was an average of four cents per pound higher in Montreal than Australian butter in London, and during the past year Canadian dairy products have ranged for 2-| cents to 3 cents per pound above the world's market price. Yet the hon. gentlemen of the Conservative party want the consumers of butter in Canada to pay a still higher price for that product. I want every consumer of butter in Canada, and more particularly the mothers of families in every town and city in this Dominion, to know that this is the policy of the Conservative party under their present leader-wanting them to pay a price higher than the world's market price, and just to that degree destroy the purchasing power of the Canadian people.
On the 25th of October of last year the hon. leader of the opposition in the city of Montreal said:
What are we doing to safeguard our agricultural life, not only for to-day but for tomorrow ?
And after referring to the importations of butter under the Australian treaty, he continued :
The dairy industry cannot be built up in a day or in a year. It is being destroyed.
His inference is that nothing is being done by this government to safeguard the agricultural life of this country. I wonder where the hon. gentleman has been sojourning when he thinks that the Canadian dairy industry is being destroyed. Has he actually sunk into such depths of real bachelordom? If any of our other bachelor leaders should develop such density we would have them married at once. That, sir, is the surest cure for any such ailment. The whole thing reminds me of an incident last June after I had put on Hansard the facts in connection with butter and the Australian treaty. I happened to meet some of my good Tory friends out in the corridor and they said: "Say, Mac, where is that butter?" " Boys," I said, " I plastered you all over from the soles of your feet to the crown of your head and you could not help yourselves. That is where the butter is." Apparently, however, their hon. leaders have never thoroughly cleansed themselves and are now living in an atmosphere of such lacteal density that their mental peregrinations are most amusing. They call to mind that divine injunction, " Man, know thyself." The greatest study of mankind is man, and, goodness knows, we members of parliament have a wonderful opportunity for study along that line. I often wonder where the hon. gentleman was browsing mentally when, in 1915, the American government removed

every restriction against the importation of Canadian finished live stock and fresh meats and also placed wheat, flour and potatoes on the tentative free list. He was then very close to the members of the Canadian government. Why did he not then show his appreciation and safeguard the live stock industry of Canada by insisting that the government remove the duty on like American products coming into this country? Is it any wonder that after five years' experience of an entire lack of appreciation, during which time the Tory government in Canada maintained an almost prohibitive duty against like American products, the American government saw fit to withdraw the privilege? That was the time when he and his political friends should have shown some concern for the interests and welfare of Canadian agriculture, but they were asleep at the switch.
However, we do occasionally get a glimpse of their hon. leader's meanderings. Speaking at Cookshire, in the province of Quebec, last summer, he said:
There should be in Canada a tariff commission such as they have in the United States . . . . This should determine the conditions under which our manufacturers and our producers have to meet the competition of the world.
According to press reports, on the 2nd of October, 1926, in his own city of Calgary, he made a similar statement:
A tariff board, such as they have in the United States, should hear all the evidence and make its recommendations. By that we stand or fall.
What kind of tariff board have they in the United States? It is in effect a tariff commission for the purpose of giving the manufacturers the full power to exploit the consumer. For instance, it investigated the sugar duties. Its report was presented to the president. From that day to this the president has failed to make that report public. So close were the big interests linked up with the operation of the tariff board in the United States that actually the representative of the sugar interests was present on the board in the person of Mr. H. H. Glassie. Common decency and common justice should have intimated to that gentleman that he should abstain from sitting on cases in which his personal interests were so apparent. But this he refused to do. Congress passed a special law removing Mr. Glassie from the payroll of the nation until the case was finished. Yet this is the kind of thing that passes for a tariff board in the United States. Naturally this aroused some storms. Investigation was threatened. Senator Smoot, one of the big

The Budget-Mr. Macdonald (Kings)
sugar men of the United States, was always on the job to block investigation. All this is mixed up with the notorious speculative sugar market of 1921 when the exploitation of the American people by the sugar trust was one of the most glaring instances of the looting of the consumer by predatory interests ever brought to the attention of the American public. Yet this is the kind of thing which the honoured leader of the great Conservative party apparently wants to have in operation in this country. Naturally very strong opinions are voiced in the United States regarding the work of the American tariff board. For instance, Dr. Taussig, of Harvard University, and a former chairman of the tariff commission, at a meeting of the American Economic Association two years ago, expressed it as his opinion that:
The interests involved in the results of tariff making were so powerful and exercised such influence upon the party in power that disinterested and non-partisan action was practically impossible.
Those are strong words, but they come from a man of calm and reasoned judgment, a man who had had experience on the tariff board, and who was by no means an opponent of tariff protection. Dr. E. P. Costigan, of Denver, who also has had experience with the tariff" board, said:
It should have turned upon it the clearest searchlight of publicity, that its past performances have little to commend it, and until it conforms to disinterested standards of public service, congress should refuse any further financial appropriation for its work.
There is the situation. Possibly the hon. gentleman would like to revive the battledore and shuttlecock methods which were in operation just before the Conservative party was defeated in the fall of 1921.
It might be interesting to lift the veil for a moment on one commodity-sugar-to disclose the true situation. To really understand the facts, it should be known that when James Murdock resigned his position as the last remaining member of the original Board of Commerce of that day he preferred serious charges against members of the cabinet. Rather than investigate those charges, the government filled the vacancies on the board by appointing three paid servants of the government. There never was a ease which showed more plainly the absurdity, the injustice, and the injury to the consuming classes of the enactment of customs duties than did this sugar monopoly in Canada. In the whole muddle one fact was clear, that the sugar trade of this country was largely in the hands 78594-54
of a group of refiners who for most purposes acted together, and who for many years had very successfully controlled the sugar situation in Canada to their own exhorbitant profit through the kindly aid of the tariff. In this particular case-I regret, Mr. Speaker, that I have exhausted my forty minutes.
Hon. JOHN A. MACDONALD (Kings): Mr. Speaker, in rising briefly to discuss the budget, I feel that the masterly criticism delivered last Thursday by the then acting leader of this party (Mr. Guthrie) covered the ground so thoroughly that the Conservative case might well be rested there. However, there are usually some local aspects to which those members who follow the leaders can give attention.
As has already been stated, the financial condition of the country is set out in the budget speech in clear and concise terms. The facts and figures are doubtless correctly stated, but the conclusions which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) seeks to draw therefrom I submit are not altogether warranted. It can easily be shown that other factors besides the so-called Robb budgets have contributed to the prosperity and increasing trade of the Dominion. It can also be shown, as the member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) pointed out this afternoon, that the much-vaunted prosperity is not as far reaching as is claimed by the government and their supporters. The prosperity is largely a paper prosperity and is confined to the larger cities. As a matter of fact the annual reports of our banks and large corporations are relied on as evidence of that prosperity, t agree with my hon. friend from York-Sunbury that if you apply the prosperity test to New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, to the farmers and fishermen of those provinces, and to many others who to-day are struggling for a livelihood, the result is not as satisfactory as the government would have us believe.
The eloquent speech of the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat (Mr. McMillan) was the most amazing example of inconsistency that I have heard this session. He opened his address by stating that everything is prosperous, but that high protection stands in the way of prosperity. He seems to overlook the fact that the government of which he is such an enthusiastic supporter are maintaining this high protection, and at the same time they lose no opportunity to proclaim the great prosperity which the country is enjoying under their beneficent control. But the hon. gentleman goes further, he character-

850	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Macdonald (Kings)
izes this high protection as embodying a vicious principle, notwithstanding the fact that the government which he has supported so unquestioningly have had the power at any time during the last seven or eight years to put an end to high protection. Then he would eliminate trade barriers. Well, apparently, he still believes in the trade theories of Bright and Cobden and their contemporaries. But those theories are entirely out of date to-day. The nations of the world are protecting their industries and striving to build up a powerful industrial system and it would be utterly impossible for Canada situated as she is, to maintain her economic position under free trade. The hon. gentleman also stated that high protection brought eighteen years of stagnation. Yet he claims that we have this wonderful prosperity under the very system which has been continued with very little change down to the present time.
The tariff policy of the new administration in the United States was also discussed by my hon. friend. But why not face the facts? Everyone is aware that last fall the outstanding feature of the policy of the Republican candidate for the presidency and his party was protection for the farmers to cover all their products. There is no question whatever about the fact that the special session of congress that has been called is to be devoted to this particular purpose.
With regard to the tariff, the Liberals have always, in my recollection, claimed that the tariff was a tax; we have had to meet that argument in all of the elections I have had anything to do with for many years past. Yet in the face of present conditions they claim that they are reducing the taxation of the country. But what do we find on looking up the figures? The last summary issued by the Department of National Revenue shows that in the ten months of the present fiscal year, up to January, 1929, the duties collected in this country amounted to $162,703,554, as compared with the duties collected for the same period in 1928 of $139,355,327, or an increase in the last ten months, in duties paid-which the Liberal party has always claimed to be a tax- of $23,348,227.
A few days ago the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) showed by figures taken from the public records that the average increase in taxation during the last five years, as compared with the last five years of Conservative rule in Canada, amounted to $51,000,000 per annum. Yet, in face of these facts, hon. gentlemen opposite will stand up and say that they are reducing taxation. The fact is that there never was a time in the history

of Canada when taxtation was as high as it is to-day by many millions of dollars; and notwithstanding the fact that they claim some credit for a reduction in the rate of taxation here and there, the situation shows that taxation has very largely increased. If this increase in taxation, resulting in increased revenue, were being economically made use of, if we were getting from it the services which the country stands most in need of, if we were obtaining a reduction in the debt to the extent that we might have by the practice of economy, then all would be well. But apparently this additional money has had the effect of tempting the government into a period of extravagant expenditure in which no amounts are too large.
I am one of those who would like to see Ottawa made beautiful; I am just as anxious as anyone else to see this done. But I do not believe that the millions of dollars voted for this purpose are being well expended, especially at the present time when the country has so many other pressing obligations, including the burden of debt which we are carrying. I do not believe that half a million -or more than half a million-expended on automobiles in this country is an economical or reasonable expenditure. And there are many others that one could cite; one could go on for an hour proving reckless and extravagant expenditures. These are but samples. Yet the government, because, as they claim, they have no money, are obliged to discontinue the technical education grant; the statement from the treasury benches is that there is no money. And they are obliged also to refuse any contribution to good roads in Canada; they have no money with which to assist the provinces along that line. But I would point out that there is no movement in this country to-day which would be of as great value to the farmers and to others who are attempting to carry on business as would be the improvement of the roads.
The last speaker (Mr. McMillan) referred to a national highway to cost $200,000,000. Why, sir, that is simply sidetracking the issue; no one would seriously consider such a thing. But there are ways and means of promoting the development of good roads in this country without tackling such a project. This Dominion, I believe, should follow the lead given by the late Conservative government when $20,000,000 was voted to assist the provinces in road work.
There is no question about the fact that if the government turned over a new leaf and practised sufficient economy they could wipe out the sales tax entirely and still not hamper the finances of the Dominion. So that, from

The Budget-Mr. Macdonald (Kings)
the standpoint of economy, they are failing; there is no doubt at all . that rank extravagance can be proved against the government.
There are many matters involved in a discussion of the budget, and among these may. be included, as important questions, markets and transportation. When we come to look at this government's work along this line we also find much room for criticism. Markets and transportation are largely complementary; they go hand in hand. And when this government established, under the British West Indies trade agreement, the Canadian National Steamship Line and put steamers on that route, they made, it seems to me, a very serious error in not including as a port of call for these steamships the city of Havana in Cuba. I realize, of course, that under the treaty as it now stands this may be difficult and perhaps impossible. But I would urge as strongly as possible on the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), who have this work in hand, the desirability of making Havana a port of call for these steamships. Probably the British West Indies would not agree, inasmuch as they are paying a subsidy in support of the service. I submit, however, that it would pay the country, it would pay-the Canadian National Steamships, to abandon that subsidy and make Cuba a port of call. What would happen? To-day these boats are going to the West Indies with very little freight; they are not half loaded. But if they were allowed to touch at Havana every cubic foot of space would be filled with potatoes every trip. That would mean that the earnings of the Canadian National Steamships would be largely increased. Moreover, it would give very much needed accommodation to the maritime provinces. The situation at the present time lends itself to monopoly in this regard. The ordinary shipper cannot ship to Havana at all: yet that is the biggest and best market we have to-day for our potatoes. That market takes 3,000.000 bushels a year from New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, but no producer can ship a bushel there unless he is big enough to charter a steamer and despatch a whole steamer load. I submit that if it is possible to make some arrangement whereby these boats could call at Havana-they pass that port within a few miles every two weeks-it would operate to the advantage of the maritimes. If this cannot be done, some other service should be established and subsidized by the government in order to provide a connection with the port of Havana.
That brings us to the general condition of the potato market at the present time, which everyone knows to be very bad. If it were not for the fact that Prince Edward Island potatoes are recognized as the best obtainable anywhere we would have had a very poor market last fall; in fact it was poor at its best, but to give you some idea of how largely the quality enters into the marketing of our crop I will just quote from the United States market report in connection with the Boston market a few days ago. The quotations show a very decided preference for Prince Edward Island stock, as follows:
Maine, 100-pound sacks, Green Mountains, United States No. 1. sacked locally, $1.20-$1.25.
Prince Edward Island, 90-pound sacks, Green Mountains A grade, $1.50-$1.75.
That condition assisted us very materially in marketing our potatoes this year, because the same preference is shown in Cuba and in the Canadian markets. Even at that, however, we cannot unload the large quantity of excellent potatoes which still remains in the hands of the farmers. In that connection I might say that we have been endeavouring to take advantage of the market which exists in western Canada; it is not a good market with regard to price but it could be made an outlet for a considerable quantity of our potatoes. In endeavouring to make use of it the Canadian National Railways did give us a very nice reduction in freight rates, but it was not sufficient to enable us to send our produce to western Canada; the freight rates were still too high although quite a few carloads were shipped. A few years ago we had a similar condition; the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) took a hand in the matter then and claimed credit for a reduction in freight rates which was given. In a circular which he sent out at that time he said:
We would add here a reminder that this movement will be in competition with selected stock imported from well-organized shippers in Minnesota and North Dakota, their shipments over shorter distances bearing lower rates, particularly to Winnipeg, but with 33 cents per one hundred pounds duty.
This winter the shippers appealed to the Canadian National Railways for a further reduction of 15 cents per hundred pounds, which would enable us to ship quite a few potatoes to the west. We were not able to obtain that reduction, but the government had it in their power to give us that 15 cents advantage by raising the duty on potatoes to 50 cents per hundred pounds, which would place it on an equality with the United States duty. If that were done we would have the advantage we
852	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Macdonald (Kings)
need in order to compete with the potatoes of North Dakota and Minnesota. That would apply to the condition of not only this year but'every year; never a year passes without many thousands of bushels of potatoes coming into Canada from the United States in the spring while our last year's crop is still in first-class condition and fit for use anywhere. I venture to say that within a month we will be offered new potatoes from Florida and Georgia in the restaurant of this house; that has happened every year in the past and probably will happen again this year, although there are millions and tens of millions of first-class potatoes in Canada which we should be eating instead of using potatoes from the United States.
These are matters to which the government should give some attention, matters with which they should deal in order to protect our farmers from this outside competition, and give them a chance against our neighbours to the south, who take advantage of our markets to dispose of their surplus products in the off-season. They should give protection when needed, something which will be stable and which will allow our farmers to carry on with a reasonable assurance that they will at least have the full benefit of the Canadian market when the foreign markets will not absorb our products.
These same arguments may be applied to the butter trade, and notwithstanding the statements of the last speaker we find that there has been an enormous change in the imports and exports of butter since the Australian treaty came into effect. We find that there has been a serious decrease in the dairying industry generally, and we all know that the number of cattle in Canada has dropped seriously. What are some of the results of this treaty from a marketing standpoint? In 1925 Canada exported about 24,500,000 pounds of butter; in four years our exports dropped to 2,056,500 pounds. These are the latest figures taken from the dairy letter issued by the Department of Agriculture and received to-day; the figures include our exports up to January of this year. Now let us consider the other side of the picture; in 1925 we imported 162,848 pounds of butter, while according to the same letter last year we imported 21,108,929 pounds, valued at over $7,000,000. The farmers of this country should have produced that butter and should have distributed that money among themselves. And the loss is not only the money lost by not producing this butter, as every farmers knows; in eastern Canada especially we are not able to keep up the fertility of the soil if we do not keep 
cattle. We must have cattle in order to maintain the fertility of the soil, so that in addition to the direct loss there is a heavy indirect loss. Practically all milk products, as well as butter, show a decrease in exports with the exception of cheese, which increased to some extent.
What is the cure for this condition? We know what we are up against; what are we to do about it? There is only one way to go about it; we must look at the whole matter from a broad national standpoint; we must endeavour to build up Canada as a whole from coast to coast with all kinds of industries and an industrial population which will provide markets for the produce of the farms. Then, if we protect these markets, the farmers will be reasonably safe. It might be said that I am speaking against foreign markets, but I am not. I have as much respect for foreign markets as any person in Canada, but they are always treacherous and tricky. If you have a well developed home market, a large consuming population of your own, then you are safe. In various parts of Canada, and especially in the maritime provinces, we have always had the Liberal party holding up before the people this policy of protection as a fearful bogey; telling them it would increase their cost of living; it would ruin them in various ways and make millionaires of all the manufacturers, and build up the cities at the expense of the country. The Liberal party has been able to put that over so successfully that practically solid delegations of Liberals have at times been returned from the maritime provinces; wholly solid from Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia and nearly so from New Brunswick. But that day is past, and the maritime provinces have awakened to the realization that they must fight for protection for their industries and see that it is provided for the rest of Canada. They have come to realize that even though they have to pay a little extra for a machine-I do not admit that this necessarily follows-which they would have to buy once in ten or fifteen years, it is better to pay that extra cost and have it manufactured in Canada. By doing that they establish a safe market for what they produce with that machine. They were told their industries had been killed by the industries of upper Canada. This was true to some extent, but we are getting our stuff much cheaper today than in the days when we were manufacturing at home in a small way. It is true we have lost our industrial population, and, as far as Prince Edward Island is' concerned we have lost over twenty per cent of our total
8o3

The Budget-Mr. Bradette
population, but we are producing more to-day with that smaller population and we are getting our stuff at a cheaper cost because of the mass production of upper Canada. Unfortunately, there is also some coming in from the United States, which has killed off our little industries.
I would like to refer to the question of old age pensions, particularly as it applies to Prince Edward Island. It has been said that I opposed old age pensions when that question was before the house in 1926. That statement is not correct. I, with others on this side, opposed the system by which the government was putting more than half the burden upon the shoulders of the provinces. We regarded that as being unfair and argued that the government should make it a federal scheme entirely. There is much difficulty in the smaller provinces with a limited revenue in taking hold of this situation. Take the position of Prince Edward Island, with its small revenue and lack of all resources from which revenue can be secured except by direct taxation on the farmers. According to population, this scheme would be more expensive there than it would be anywhere else in Canada. Many of our young people leave during the producing age and we have a smaller proportion of that class in our community than is to be found in any other province in Canada. The following comparative statement is taken from the census of 1921:

From the above tabulation it will be seen that Prince Edward Island has a much larger percentage of population from 10 to 19 years than the rest of Canada. But when we come to the ages of 20 to 44 years, which are the best producing years, we find that Prince Edward Island has a lower average than the rest of Canada. The population coming under this class are producing revenue in the other provinces, they have left Prince Edward Island and we lose in that respect. In the classification of 44 to 69 years Prince Edward Island heads the list again, and when we come to 70 years and over it is found that Prince Edward Island has a very much larger percentage than the rest of Canada. It can be seen quite easily that Prince Edward Island would have considerable difficulty in undertaking the carrying out of the old age pensions scheme. I still believe that this should have been undertaken by the federal government, because provinces like Prince Edward Island, which may not be able to undertake it, will have to contribute towards the scheme for the benefit of the other provinces.
I would like to refer to the work of the Department of National Revenue with special reference to the prevention of smuggling. In order that the house may have some idea of just what the conditions are in Prince Edward Island, I wish to read an article which appeared in the Charlottetown Patriot, on January ISth. This paper is an out-and-out suporter of the government. The article is as follows:
Laxity in Enforcement
We all know that smuggling is rampant not only here but elsewhere, and that bootlegging is constantly on the increase, while the number of places that it is rumoured in which liquor can be procured either by telephone message or personally are said to be constantly multiplying. Further, it is declared that in many of these places liquor is sold by the glass, as well as by the bottle.
It is a well known fact that for the past three years there has been more smuggling of liquor than previously, and as a natural consequence more people should be fined.
I would like the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) to take note of this statement as put forward by a newspaper which is an ardent supporter of his government. I suggest that something be done in connection with this very serious situation. We who live there, surrounded as we are by water, with opportunities for the vessels to get into every creek, bay and river, know that there never was a time in the history of the province when there was as much liquor floating around as there was last year. I would urge upon the minister that in making arrangements for the coming year he take this fact into consideration and make some effort to enforce the laws in this respect.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I speak on the budget and its amendment I would like to make a few remarks with reference to a question which has come to the forefront in the province of Ontario, more particularly since the beginning of this session. I refer to the activities of the Ontario Prohibition Union. In the past few weeks circular letters have been received from organizations working to assist the United States in preventing Canadian liquor from entering that country. I have always been an advocate of temperance and I am always prepared to sponsor and further true temperance. At the same time I cannot see why we Canadians should be called upon to enforce United States law. I have read

The Budget-Mr. Bradette

many comments in both wet and dry papers in the United States, and they are firmly convinced that the Canadian government is following the proper course in that respect. It is a well known fact that the officers of the United States government have a right to enter any ship on this side of the line and examine the papers before the ship is released, and it is also a well known fact that they have access to all boats, whether Canadian or American, on the other side of the line. It is also a well known fact that unlimited quantities of intoxicating liquor are finding their way into the United States from Cuba, which is a protectorate of that country. Cuba is yearly shipping enormous quantities of-intoxicating liquor, and apparently no checks are being used against such a practice. But I consider that the demands made to the Canadian government by the United States were absolutely unwarranted; they should have made the same demands to Great Britain and France. It is a well known fact that even under the Volstead Act liquor is being used for sacramental and also medicinal purposes in the United States. The government of the United States through its dispensaries has been receiving tens of millions of dollars in the sale of liquor. Therefore I am convinced, as one of the leading temperance men in northern Ontario, that the government in this instance is following the proper course. It must also be considered that the exportation of spirituous liquors from Canada to the United States represents only two per cent of the total consumption, so they must get it much more extensively from other sources.
The budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), with the facts and figures contained in it, speaks very eloquently of the present prosperity of Canada. In all parts of the country we find a spirit of optimism that can be brought about only by a general improvement in business. It is noted with great satisfaction that every year since 1923 has seen a decrease in the net debt of the Dominion, the reduction this year amounting to more than $50,000,000. As the interest on the funded debt at the present time represents about one-quarter of the yearly revenues of the country, this debt reduction from year to year makes possible an ever-increasing reduction in taxation and at the same time larger expenditures on the necessary developments of the country.
We are also pleased to note that the Dominion bond issues maturing during the year have been paid instead of being renewed and by following the same policy in future it should not be necessary to renew any bond

issues until 1933. As I have said, the country seems to be well satisfied; and this budget, the same as the five previous ones, has been accepted by the country as a whole, as a "Robb" budget, meaning by that that there is keen satisfaction with it throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion.
It was acknowledged by the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) in a magnificent oratorical effort, that we are experiencing prosperity. A person has only to glance over some of the headings in the newspapers and periodicals of the country to realize to a very large extent that we are really experiencing prosperity. Let me quote a few of them coming from the industrial issue of the Ottawa Journal:
General expansion placed pulp and paper industry in unusually good position.
Annual review of industry shows expansion in newsprint production more rapid than consumption-exports to countries other than United States increase-New laboratory in Montreal.
This is another one:
High mark for construction reached in past twelve months is likely to be maintained.
Normal building year now exceeds 1912 boom -building likely to continue at present levels- Ontario leads all other provinces.
Another one:
Wide distribution of bank assets make for safety and permanence unaffected by market conditions. Underlying conditions of trade today make for greater stability of Canadian banking institutions as compared to conditions at confederation.
Over 211 million bushels grain handled by harbour of Montreal but limit by no paeans reached. Is world's premier grain shipping port, having reached new record during past summer-many improvements under way including port for aircraft.
Record wheat yield of year outstanding contribution to present prosperous era. All previous records broken states C.P.R. president, who is most optimistic-he believes time has come when immigration regulations should be relaxed.	_
West is entering industrial field with oil and mining also prominent states president of national lines.	.
Prairie provinces outgrown period when agriculture only industry-new records made by C.N.R. in 1928-extensions made and services improved.
Advance in Canada's foreign trade one of outstanding achievements in modern economic development.
Noted banker reviews export trade which has developed 100 per cent since 1913-recognizes value of great tourist expenditure.
There is one particularly from northern Ontario-:
Continued progress is noted with the Lake Superior corporation. Public shows great interest.

The Budget-Mr. Bradette
Various subsidiaries making up huge indus-tral group reveal pronounced trend toward increased activities-scope of companies is broadened.
Canada's advance is outstanding in present day economic history while future is full of promise.
Statistics prove achievements were not equalled by people of any other country- bumper crops one of chief factors in financial situation in which all classes shared-advances in mineral development.
General anticipation is that present wave wilt continue during first six months of 1929 at least
It is true that the opposition maintain that this is all due to Providence, but I believe in the fine old idea that the Lord helps him who helps himself. While the administration has much to do with the present situation, there is a spirit of cooperation throughout every part of the country, and I feel certain that the people have more confidence in the present administration than they had in that of a few years ago.
I was amazed to hear some of the criticisms levelled by the acting leader of the opposition at some of the reductions in taxation, particularly when he stated that the government, in removing the tax from Pullman tickets, were helping only the richer class. In the part of the country which I have the honour to represent they do not regard it is a luxury to buy berth accommodation when they travel from northern Ontario to Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal, so this is helping the working and travelling class as a whole. The same thing applies to the criticism levelled against the reduction in the tax on cables and telegrams. The hon. gentleman said that this was going to benefit only the big corporation. But the larger corporations have always the happy peculiarity of unloading every possible tax on the public as a whole, and this principle applies also on telegrams and cables.
I listened with a good deal of attention to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross), the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie), and this afternoon to the hon. member for Vancouver-Bur-rard (Mr. Clark), in regard to the exportation of raw pulpwood to the United States to the amount of 1,500,000 cords a year. One thing every hon. member must have in mind is the fact that raw pulpwood to a settler is the finished product. I was in full sympathy with the action that was taken by the premiers of Quebec and Ontario in calling a pulpwood conference to discuss the situation in which the newsprint industry has found itself in the way of over-production and lack of market. We all know that prices were pared to such an extent that in many eases dividends could not be paid. I would be the last man to put too heavy demands on the
newsprint industry. In the constituency which I represent we have three pulp and paper corporations: the Iroquois Falls Pulp and Paper Company, Limited, The Mattagami Pulp and Paper Company and the Spruce Falls Pulp and Paper Company, which have a daily capacity of 1,300 tons of finished newsprint. Therefore I would be the last man to wish anything harmful to that industry. One thing that surprised me was the fact that the premiers of those two provinces did not see their way clear to have the pulpwood producers or the settlers represented at that conference. I have under my hand figures giving the actual cost of the pulpwood production to the newsprint industry. This is given by the companies themselves.

For the same quantity of wood, the same size of pulpwood, not delivered at the mill, the price is $5.75 to the settler. I believe there is an anomaly there which should be remedied as rapidly as possible. I would be the last man to be in favour of a policy of price-fixing, but at the same time I was absolutely in favour of the two premiers of Ontario and Quebec calling a conference, because the newsprint industry was not receiving a fair remuneration for the finished product.
During the course of last week in the Ontario legislature, the Minister of Lands and Forests in putting a bill through that body said that in northern Ontario the worst enemy of the forest was the settler. I believe that in respect to some instances may have been right, but I have no doubt that generally speaking he was wrong on that score. But if the settler of northern Ontario is the enemy of the forest, it is simply on account of the fact that he is not able to realize a sufficient price for his product. Up in that country there is what we call the clay belt, an area of 35,000 square miles. It is one of the best rural sections in the whole of the country. They have plenty of pulpwood up in that section but. as far as I have been able to ascertain, the settlers have never been able to receive a fair price for that product. So you will readily understand why the settlers are not trying to save the forests. There was exported to the United States last year 1,500.000 cords of pulpwood; and it is indeed surprising to learn that American buyers come hundreds and thousands of miles to buy that wood and pay a higher price for it than do

The Budget-Mr. Bradelte
the local buyers. The settlers have no remedy in such a situation. They have to find an outlet for their product in some way or other.
I would urge upon this government the necessity of calling a conference between the settlers and representatives of the pulpwood industry. I know that I am talking shop now, but this is a very important problem and one that should be dealt with if we are to advance the colonization of northern Ontario.
I desire to congratulate the Finance minister on the reduction of duties on mining equipment. That is just one instance showing that high duties are not always wise, are not always best for the development of any district, especially a new district like northern Ontario. We see it quite often in the newspapers that the empire is looking northward. Most of our present day development is in that north country, getting farther and farther away from the large industrial centres. We hear of large mining corporations. One of the hon. members to-day spoke of one of those companies being capitalized at one billion dollars. It is true that these companies are investing large amounts of money, but it is also true that people going into the mining game are gambling purely and simply. True, a lot of those ventures have turned out all right, but others have not turned out quite so well. This government must help the people in northern Ontario. I myself have received many letters from organizations like the Hollinger and other mining corporations, first, pleading for a reduction of the duty on their mining equipment, and later congratulating the Finance minister upon the reduction of duties of mining equipment in general.
Some big mining men in Toronto and Montreal have started up an industry, that of manufacturing mining machinery. It is true that some of their equipment is purchased here in Canada, but in almost every instance the equipment is purchased either in Great Britain or in the United States, and I am pleased to say that the mining interests in northern Ontario are perfectly satisfied with the reductions that have been made.
It seems to me that pur friends oq the other side think that they have a cure for all ills. One member said to-night there was no mention of protection at the last Conservative convention at Winnipeg. During the whole of last session I remember very well some of the members on this side tantalizing members on the other side as to what they meant by certain expressions, but hon. gentlemen opposite would never commit themselves.

Ever since the session the leader of the opposition has been going up and down practically every section of the country telling the people that the only solution he could offer was higher protection. But I must state with all frankness, as a representative of northern Ontario, that the people of that part of the country realize that this government has the only real policy in connection with tariff. We realize also that this government is not satisfied with the tariff policy that was good for this country fifteen or twenty years ago. We realize, however, that this government is formulating a tariff policy applicable for this year just the same as the tariff of twenty years ago was applicable to the needs of the country at that time.
On account of our geographical situation, we Should be free traders, but we are fully alive to the needs and requirements of governmental administration-, the revenue for which must partly be raised by indirect taxation or collection of customs duties. We produced last year thirteen hundred tons of finished1 newsprint daily and it would be absolutely impossible for northern Ontario, or for that matter, the whole of the province of Ontario, to consume even a very small proportion of that newsprint. Of necessity, we must go to the outside markets of the world. Not only that, but on account of being a -new section of the country, and being quite a distance away from the industrial centres, we must naturally buy on a high tariff market all the commodities that we require. But we are perfectly satisfied to play the game with the rest of the country. We believe that under some circumstances a certain amount of protection is required in connection with a new industry, and we need a tariff for revenue purposes. Hon. friends opposite would seek to put up a high tariff that would not be acceptable to the whole of New Ontario-. At the present time, we must export. Take our mining industry; it must find its outlet in- t'he markets of the world. Our newsprint industry must find its outlet in the markets of the world, and high protection is absolutely a policy and a principle that I am positive my hon. friends opposite were they in power, would never dare to apply to that section of the country which I have the honour to represent.
With regard to vegetables and fruits, I do not believe that we will ever be able in that section of the country to produce a sufficient quantity to supply the needs of the people there, or the people of Ontario. However, the growers should have protection. I believe that the British Columbia growers have suf-

The Budget-Mr. Bradette
ficient protection in connection with their industry. There is one thing, however, that puzzles me, and that is that we have to pay such excessive prices for British Columbia fruit. In northern Ontario, in the winter time, for instance, we have to pay 25 cents for three British Columbia apples, yet the growers of British Columi'ba claim that they have not sufficient protection.	There was
quite a movement inaugurated last fall by the fruit growers of British Columbia, complaining of the fact that there was practically no tariff protection extended to the fruit growers of this country. As I was very much interested in that question, I took the trouble to make an inquiry into the matter, and to my astonishment I found that we had a higher rate of protection against American fruit than they had against us. I will just give a list of eight fruits to corroborate that statement. Let us assume that a Canadian importer imports one thousand pounds of each
