So at the present time the fruit industry is fully protected. There are times when we have to pay, in northern Ontario, as much as fifty cents a pound for tomatoes. Someone must be making a certain amount of money at such a price.
As I say, we are perfectly satisfied to play the game with other sections of the country, but at the same time I am firmly convinced that higher tariffs will be no solution of the situation in this part of the country. . I believe this government is following the proper course, a business course, a course that will be beneficial to all1 concerned.
I do not intend to deal at any length with what the United States are going to do in connection with their tariff. It amused me, however, this afternoon, to hear some of the hon. members opposite mention the fact that the Minister of Finance waited until Friday to place his budget before the house; that he
should have brought it down after the inaugural speech of the president of the United States. I do not see the logic of that argument, and I do not see why we should time our actions in accordance with theirs. I for one am not dreading the situation as some of the hon. members opposite seem to dread it. As has been well said by one member on this side of the house to-day, I fully believe the United States are going to maintain the amicable relations they have had with us in the past, even on tariff matters. We must also consider that there are two schools of thought in the United States the same as here in Canada on that question. It is true that perhaps some farmers situated near the border on the American side will benefit by an increase in tariffs on Canadian farm products, but as the urban population in the United States is much larger than the rural population, so I am not apprehensive of that movement. It would be a movement that would be resented by the majority of the people of that country which sentiment the American politician must take into consideration.
Now, even if the United States do increase their tariff at the special session of congress next month I do not believe it would be prudent for us to take such steps as. would simply increase the cost of living in this country. Speaking for a large section of northern Ontario, I am positive that if the Canadian tariff is raised we are going to pay for it in good Canadian dollars. But I have sufficient confidence in this government to realize that they will deal in a logical way with whatever situation may develop. In this connection I may be permitted to quote certain authorities. Writing in Barron's Weekly, Sir George Paish expresses the following opinion:
The world cannot enjoy political peace in a condition of economic war. The great world conference convened by the League of Nations, in affirming that- "no machinery for the settlement of international disputes can be relied upon to maintain peace if the economic policies of the world so develop as to create not only deep divergencies of economic interest between different masses of the world's population but a sense of intolerable injury and injustice," stated a truth that cannot be doubted. Political peace is impossible without economic peace, and economic cooperation. The nations must work together for the common good. No nation can live at the expense of another.
In the bankers' plea for the removal of restrictions on European trade, it was wisely stated that our neighbours are our customers, and that their well-being is essential to our own welfare. The world economic conference affirmed this truth in language that cannot be misunderstood. But the nations, by their . actions, are still unconvinced of its truth.
The Budget-Mr. Brndette

Indeed, they seem to be convinced that it is untrue. Trade restrictions and tariffs are still being increased in many directions. Even in Great Britain "safeguarding" is being extended. The whole world is pursuing a policy of trade restriction, the effect of which is the exact reverse of that which the situation demands.
The principle here enunciated applies also to Canada to-day. It may be true that the American tariff will be raised on certain commodities that we now export to the United States, but it is not certain that any substantial increases will be made. My other authority is Sir Herbert Holt-a practical man,, not a theorist. At the annual meeting of the shareholders of the Royal Bank of Canada he said:
In spite of the fact that the present trade relationship between the two countries-
Referring to the United States and Canada.
-is disproportionately favourable to the United States, there is active discussion of further tariff increases that seem likely to shut out the few competitive items which Canadians now sell there. It would seem that those who propose such tariff changes fail to realize that checks upon Canadian prosperity automatically cheek the volume of goods which can be bought from the United States, and that on the other hand continued improvement in Canadian conditions brings corresponding increases in the volume of goods which they can sell us. From this viewpoint it might be considered economic statesmanship for the United States to discover means to increase their purchases from Canada, [DOT]rather than to consider measures which will constitute new trade barriers.
Moreover, it is not feasible for a country to sever completely foreign polijey from tariff policy. Official observers from the United States at the world economic conference at Geneva, and influential representatives of the United States Chamber of Commerce at the meeting of the international chamber of Commerce at Stockholm, expressed disapproval of such measures as would be likely to hinder the flow of international trade. With other nations looking to the United States for assistance in reconstructing the world's economic organization, the proposed tariff increases would constitute a severe blow at international economic cooperation and goodwill.
If further handicaps are placed upon the exports of Canada to the United States, it will be imperative for Canadians to seek more favourable trade agreements-
No mention of higher tariff.
-with other nations and to change the present relationship by the application of measures for their own protection. As a last resort, it may be necessary to meet this situation by direct tariff increases and by granting further preference to Great Britain and to most-favoured-nations. This is not a statement in favour of exhorbitant tariffs. I am not suggesting tariffs which will increase the cost of living in Canada, but rather such measures as will permit the continued growth of Canadian production and stimulate trade relationships with those coun-[Mr. Bradette.I
tries who are willing to buy agricultural and other products from this country on terms which will permit the maintenance of a reasonable and stable prosperity.
Those are practically the words of the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. There is no mention of retaliation. No one will dare say that Sir Herbert Holt is a dreamer. His practical views should be very carefully considered before we go on the rampage with respect to tariff matters. By hasty retaliatory measures, instead of penalizing our friends to the south we might penalize our own people.
Now, Mr. Speaker, a few words on immigration. At the outset I may say that I firmly believe Premier Ferguson is a friend of northern Ontario, as is also his Minister of Lands and Forests. Northern Ontario is a wonderful part of the province, immense in area, and richly endowed with minerals, with water-powers and with forest resources. It is also one of the best agricultural sections, the 35,000 square mile clay belt being admirably adapted for settlement. At the same time I do not think an immigration scheme on a large scale will be feasible in that country. I presume all members of this house are familiar with the failure of the Kapuskasing colonization experiment, on which the provincial government spent millions of dollars. Unfortunately, the immigrants were not familiar with farming conditions in northern Ontario and did not become acclimatized, and of course they failed to make good. In fact the government had to transfer those people to Toronto and other large centres. Recently I read in the December issue of the Empire Review an article by Premier Ferguson in which he described the kitchen garden farms of Denmark. Speaking of the size of these farms the Premier of Ontario said that they were from 15 to 50 acres in area. Had he visited that country four or five years ago, I would have been inclined to believe that he had tried to apply the same principle to northern Ontario. About five years ago, and apparently without any consultation with the settlers of that section of the province the size of the farms was reduced from 150 to 75 acres. But those small farms would not be suitable in northern Ontario. Not a single farmer from the older portion of the province would attempt farming in northern Ontario on such a small scale. Everybody familiar with a timber farm will tell you that allowance must be made for a certain amount of waste land. In clearing such a farm the pioneer must select an elevated spot on which to build his home and start farming operations, and eventually he gets access to the lower

The Budget-Mr. Campbell
lying land, but almost invariably there is a good deal of rocky land which cannot be brought under cultivation. I am sorry that I cannot air my views on this subject in the provincial legislature, and therefore I must take this opportunity to do so here. I submit that northern Ontario is not equipped to take care of a large immigrant population. In many sections where the people have been on their farms for ten or fifteen years they are still without roads and therefore have no access to markets. I have stated that they are not getting a fair remuneration for their pulpwood, and it is absolutely necessary that they should, because they rely upon this for their living. The farmer depends upon his pulpwood for himself and his family. So that we must be very careful in dealing with this matter. We are also trying to get agriculturists to come to Canada, and we know that eventually 50 per cent of them will find their way to the larger centres.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I
do not propose to enter into a general discussion of the whole budget, but I desire to deal with a matter which I consider to be of paramount importance at the present time; and in this connection may I quote from the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) delivered in this house on February 16, 1928-that is to say, the budget speech of last year. The remarks to which I wish to call the attention of the house will be found at page 513 of Hansard of that year:
In order to foster empire trade there is a general tendency in the Dominions and the mother country to increase the percentage of cost of production requirements on goods receiving the benefit of the British preferential tariff. At present Canada requires 25 per cent to be empire labour and materials. It is proposed to double this percentage. There will be similar increases in the percentages required on goods entering under treaty rates and the intermediate tariff.
Now I will not accuse the Minister of Finance of attempting to deceive the house, but I did receive an entirely wrong impression because, when I began to study the situation, I came to the conclusion that this regulation would have exactly the opposite effect. Speaking in this house on February 27, 1928, I drew the attention of the minister to that fact. May I be permitted to quote briefly from the remarks I made on that occasion. I said:
Ninety per cent of the short staple cotton used in British mills is purchased outside the empire. 30 per cent of the total American exports of cotton going to the United Kingdom.
Not more than 15 to 20 per cent of the cost of the finished product of the British cotton mills is labour.
I pointed out that the effect of this regulation would be to debar British manufactured cottons from the benefits of the British preference. It might be that when the raw cotton was very low in price the labour and other materials might happen to be 50 per cent or more of the cost, and under these circumstances these cottons might come in under the British preference. But when cotton prices were high certainly cotton manufactured goods from Great Britain would be debarred from the benefits of the British preference. I pointed out that in effect the Minister of Finance was saying to the consumers of Canada that when cotton prices were low the duty might remain as it was, but that when cotton prices were high he proposed to increase the tariff. In fact, I quoted some figures, which I will read at the present moment.
In ten years the average value of the raw cotton used in British mills was 46 per cent of the finished value of the goods. In one year it was about 58 per cent. It is quite obvious, then, that under this new proposal the advantage of the British preference will largely be lost to the British cotton manufacturers.
.On February 29, two days later, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) was addressing the house on the budget and I presume he was referring to my remarks when he said, as reported at page 893 of Hansard:
As to the criticism which has been uttered with respect to the intimation by the Minister of Finance that in future it was proposed to ask that all goods coming in, taking advantage of the British preference, should have a 50 per cent British or empire content. I desire to say just this: the Minister of Finance gave that intimation in no sense intending thereby to limit the British preference in the slightest degree.
Further on he said:
Some hon. gentleman in the far corner-I forget who it was-instanced the possibility that the raising of the limit to 50 per cent might have the effect of debarring British goods. I can assure my hon. friend on the authority of the Minister of Finance that there is no intention to permit it to be used for any such purpose, and if as a result of experience it is found necessary to provide a different percentage of content for different classes of goods, as other British dominions have done, it is quite within the competency of the government to work out the solution along those lines.
That assurance seemed fairly definite. But that is not all. On March 13 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), speaking in the same budget debate, made further reference

The Budget-Mr. Campbell

to this matter. Referring to this provision regarding the British preference, he said:
May I say this to the house:	If we discover,
in connection with the enforcement of a regulation of that kind, that the consumers of this country are in any particular losing the benefits which the British preference was intended to give, we shall not hesitate speedily to make such changes as the circumstances may demand.
Then the Prime Minister proceeded to deal with what I presume were my remarks, in which the suggestion was made that when cotton prices were high that was the very time the duty would be raised; and concluding on that particular point the right hon. gentleman said:
I wish to say that if that situation arises it is not the intention of the government to make the existing 25 per cent British content 1 per cent higher than it is at the present time.
Now these remarks of the two ministers cannot be misunderstood, and for my part I went home after last session feeling assured that this provision would not be carried into effect. Imagine my surprise, however, when on the first of February this year the provision, without being modified or amended to any degree, was put into effect. And it is in operation at the present time.
Some protests have been made by the British High Commissioner and by the British Federation of Industries over the enforcement of this provision. Their opposition is based, of course, on the opinion that it will debar some British goods from the benefits of the preference. On March 4, a week ago, I secured an order from this house for the return of correspondence between the government and the British High Commissioner and between the government and the British Federation of Industries with respect to this matter. I regret that although one week has elapsed I have not received these papers. On Saturday morning I called at the minister's office and was told that they were all ready, but the minister had not given his authority for them to be turned over to me. Of course I am not suggesting that he was withholding them until after this debate, but certainly the matter has been overlooked. I am sorry that these papers are not in my hands, because I should then be in a better position to deal with the question. At the present time the only information I have with respect to the protests made by the British High Commissioner and the British Federation of Industries is what I have gleaned from the newspapers. May I quote from the Manitoba Free Press of February 11 last. In a rather lengthy article dealing with this provision and its effects on interimperial trade the following appears:

Imports of cotton under the preferential tariff will be radically restricted unless the new regulations are modified. Efficiency of cotton spinning, weaving and finishing in England is so great that in many of the early stages of manufacture the cost of raw cotton, 20 cents a pound at the present time, is more than 50 per cent of the sale price of the article. Under the new regulations various cotton goods will be unable to qualify for the British preferential tariff.
And further on:
In the case of low count yarns, for example, the preferential tariff is 10 per cent and the general tariff 20 per cent. Grey cotton fabrics are dutiable at 12J per cent preferential and 22J per cent general.
This means actually doubling the tariff on many articles of cotton manufacture. Further on the article draws attention to the fact that Canada's importations of semi-manufactured and manufactured cotton goods in 1928 approximated $33,000,000. It goes on to say that ' this trade is divided between Great Britain and the United States; the British trade is almost entirely in manufactured goods while the United States trade is at least partly in semi-manufactured goods; and in conclusion the article says:
Therefore the new regulations, unless modified, will be of assistance to the Canadian textile industry.
On this point there is no dispute; the Canadian textile manufacturers are well aware of this feature of the new policy which, by the way, they are strongly supporting. The Canadian Textile Journal of January 17 says:
The new regulation is a progressive step and it should be enforced without qualification or equivocation.
Again I quote from the Manitoba Free Press of February 12, which contained an article dealing with the various commodities which will be affected by this provision. First there is the question of copper, and the article quotes from a memorandum presented to the minister by the British Federation of Industries:
"It is true," says the memorandum, "that copper is imported into Great Britain from within the British Empire but the main source of the world's supply is the United States of America. With the best of intentions British manufacturers will be quite unable to certify that any finished copper article exported to Canada is made of Australian copper and still less of copper from any other part of the empire, for the simple reason that firms importing copper cannot segregate supplies coming from one particular source or another."
Then it refers to the fur industry :
Still another industry to be affected will be fur manufacturing. There are no raw furs produced in the United Kingdom, and while quantities are brought, from Canada, a large part comes from Russia.

The Budget-Mr. Campbell
Then it refers to the matter of velvet, and says:
The raw material of velvet comes from China and Japan and is brought to England where it is woven. Then it is sent to Germany to be fabricated and back to England to be finished.
Then it refers to boots and shoes, and says:
It seems that much of the raw material going into British boots and shoes-leather raw hides-comes from the Argentine. To most people it will seem incredible that the cost of the raw leather should exceed 50 per cent of the cost of the finished product, but it is so represented in Ottawa. No doubt the cheaper grades of boots and shoes are more particularly affected.
Let us analyse these particular items; first there is the question of copper. Under ordinary circumstances it might be said that this provision would compel the British manufacturer to use Canadian raw copper, but at present this will be of no benefit to Canadian copper producers because, as hon. members know, there is a world shortage of copper. Just now it is not a matter of selling our copper; the output has been sold for months ahead, and all the copper mines in the world cannot keep up with the demands of the industry. Copper has risen over 50 per cent in the markets of the world during the last six months, so for that reason this provision will be of no benefit to the copper industry.
Then we come to cotton, and there seems to be no question but that the British cotton manufacturer must purchase his raw material in the United States, which debars cotton from the benefits of the British preference altogether. This affects not only Great Britain but also Australia, New Zealand, Czechoslovakia and France, countries which now enjoy special treaty tariffs.
I would like to point out that from what I have gleaned from the press the British High Commissioner has been very moderate in his demands. He is not asking the Canadian government to repeal this regulation; he simply asks the government that all materials not produced economically within the empire should bo exempt and that a list of the articles so exempt should be published as has been done in Australia land New Zealand. I may say that cotton is an outstanding example of these articles. Now may I quote again from a London despatch appearing in the Manitoba Free Press of January 21, as follows:
The British overseas trade department confesses itself surprised at the discovery that certain cotton goods exported to Canada from Lancashire cannot claim more then 50 per cent of their value to be due to British labour. An
important official said to me:	"I make it my
business to watch all that concerns trade relations with Canada and when the regulation requiring 50 per cent qualification for preferential tariff was announced it never occurred to me that textiles would be affected. There wSre some goods affected of relatively small importance, perhaps only one British firm would be supplying them to Canada, but in this case of cotton it affects Lancashire. I find that the goods causing the difficulty are grey cloths. Haw cotton comes here, is spun and woven and then sent to Canada for bleaching and dyeing. You will see that last year Canada imported nearly 29,000,000 yards of greys, of which more than 9,000,000 went from Britain. It is almost the largest item in our cotton trade with Canada and the new regulation will drive the trade to the Lnited States.
Now I would like to quote again from an Ottawa despatch appearing in the Montreal Gazette of January 18. This includes many figures which go to show that the effect of this provision will be to drive that trade to the United States rather than to Great Britain. It states:
During the first six months of the present fiscal year, Canada imported from the United Kingdom yarns and threads to the value of $2,136,714,'an increase of $300,000, as compared with the corresponding six months last year. This trade will be greatly handicapped if not entirely shut off under the regulation effective on February 1 next. On yarns over forties single. Britain has recently been taking the Canadian import trade away from the United States owing to the British preference, the customs duties being 10 per cent on goods from the United Kingdom and 15 per cent on goods from the United States.
Further oh there are figures which tend to prove this contention, and then the article proceeds:
The change a fortnight hence will undoubtedly result in dwindling imports from the mother land and increased purchases from the United States. British manufacturers claim that they are helpless, for they must import their raw cotton from the United States. -
If there were any doubts as to the ultimate effects of this regulation and as to the sources from which pressure was brought to bear upon the minister, those doubts may be set at rest by an editorial appearing in the Canadian Textile Journal of November 29 last, which states in part:
Manufacturers and producers will welcome the announcement from Ottawa that after February 1 goods to enjoy the British preference entering Canada will be required to be 50 per cent of empire material and labour, instead of 25 per cent as at present. The new ruling, which was forecast in the last budget, also applies to goods coming into Canada from other countries enjoying special treaty privileges, in which case goods must contain at least 50 per cent of the labour and material of the country from whence imported.

The Budget-Mr. Campbell
I would like to quote further from an article dealing with this regulation which appeared in the same issue of the Canadian Textile Journal:
This increase in empire content was foreshadowed by Hon. James A. Robb in his last budget and is due to the repeated demand of Canadian producers. -
So there should be no doubt whatever as to the source from which came the pressure. I hold in my hand a memorandum which was sent to the minister two years ago by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association recommending this very provision, with the exception that in some cases they requested a 75 per cent content instead of 50 per cent. Apparently this memorandum was turned over to the tariff board on May 5, 1926, and it seems not to have been heard by the board at all. Just here I want to point out what I consider a serious discrimination on the part of the minister. A year ago the United Farmers of Canada sent a delegation to wait on the minister asking for certain tariff changes which they considered in the interests of their industry. The minister refused to listen to them and said they must go before the tariff board. It now appears that these textile manufacturers were allowed in by the back door; they were not obliged to go before the tariff board and place their cards upon the table, but when the farmers asked the same thing they were curtly told they must place their case before the board. The following appears in an editorial of the Canadian Textile Journal of December 6th, 1928:
There is still much to be done on the question of the textile tariff, and it is gratifying to learn that the wool cloth items wll be reviewed again shortly either in a public or private enquiry, but it is our opinion that having stated its case publicly this branch of the industry will gain more through private conference with the Commissioner of Customs than by further public reiteration of its adverse condition.
Apparently they were speaking from experience.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If I understood the hon.
member correctly, he made the statement that a deputation from the United Farmers of Canada came down to lay their case before the government and were refused a hearing and told to go before the tariff board. I was present at that meeting, and I think the Prime Minister was there, as well as the Minister of Finance and other ministers. Those men made their statement before a committee of parliament, so they were heard when they came to Ottawa.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They must have been
told their case could not be considered, because certain members of that delegation came to us and informed us that the minister told them they would have to lay their case . before the tariff board. My complaint is that there is discrimination here; these other gentlemen were not obliged to go before the tariff board with their case. I would just as soon have it heard by a committee of ministers as by the tariff board, as long as there was no discrimination in the matter.
The following appears in an editorial in the Saskatoon Star of February 15. This editorial deals with the change which was announced in the method of applying the British tariff, and says:
When the change was announced it was remarked here that the effect wrould be simply to cut down the advantage enjoyed by British manufacturers in this market, and just to that extent, to discourage British imports into Canada.
The editorial goes on to itemize the various commodities affected, and in conclusion says:
Unless something like this is done, the change which occurred this month will be in effect nothing more than a straight increase of tariff taxation on British goods of several sorts. Increases in tariff taxation of any kind are certainly not in line with the declared policy of the government, nor are they demanded by the Canadian public. Least of all is there any call for higher duties on goods from Britain. Our trade with Britain now shows a very heavy balance in favour of Canada. If any change is to be made in the tariff levied on goods from the United Kingdom, the preference should be increased and not cut down. One may expect to see the government questioned on the matter during this session.
I would like to quote from the speech delivered by the minister (Mr. Robb) in this house on March 1, as follows:
Canada, the pioneer of the British preference, looks on empire trade as the key-stone of its external trade policy and desires in every way to foster closer trading relations throughout the British commonwealth of nations.
In this instance I think the actions of the minister belie his words. The minister continues:
As the years go by an increasing quantity of our domestic production must necessarily be marketed abroad. It is our desire to trade freely with any and all who are willing to trade with us.
That has been taken throughout the country, and I believe throughout the United States, as a gentle hint to the new government of the United States. But the same kind of hint may be given to us by Great Britain, because we are in precisely the same position with respect to that country as are the United

The Budget-Mr. Campbell
States with respect to Canada. On reference to the official trade report of the Department of Trade and Commerce, I find that our total imports from the United States in the year 1928 amounted to $825,740,612, while our exports to the United States amounted to $492,541,120. This leaves what we commonly call an unfavourable trade balance of $333,199,492. This figure is really increased in another way.
I noticed an article in the Financial Times of March 8, taken from the Wall Street Journal, protesting against any raise in the tariff on Canadian goods and pointing out that Canada is not only one of the United States' best customers for manufactured goods, but is also one of the best customers for its money. The article stated that up to the end of 1928 there was an investment of United States money in Canada amounting to $3,250,000,000. Taking an annual dividend of about five per cent on that amount, which should be paid by the shipment of goods to the United States, it will be seen that it would increase our unfavourable trade balance to about half a billion dollars. The trade reports show that our imports of cotton from the United States in 1928 amounted to $44,171,933, but of this amount $27,107,186 represents raw cotton, which leaves a balance of $17,064,747 in manufactured goods. I find that our imports from the United Kingdom for the same year amounted to $190,712,351, while our exports amounted to $447,883,646, leaving what is commonly called a favourable trade balance of $257,171,295. This is a trade we should foster and not put into effect regulations which will tend to destroy that favourable trade balance. We imported manufactured cotton from Great Britain to the value of $13,593,034, and our exports to Great Britain of grain and grain products amounted to $325,092,144.
Anything which will tend to interfere with the trade between Canada and England will be fraught with serious consequences for our grain trade. At the present time Great Britain is practically the only market we have for our grain and grain products. It is absurd to say that Great Britain must buy our grain, because there are other countries producing grain. Russia may be in a position in a short time to supply a great deal of the British market, and these other countries are prepared to buy dollar for dollar from Great Britain for the grain they sell. I would like to quote from a speech of Sir Herbert Holt delivered recently at the annual shareholders meeting of the Royal Bank of Canada. Referring to the agitation in the United States for an increase in the duties against Canadian products, he says:
It would seem that those who propose such tariff changes fail to realize that checks upon Canadian prosperity check the volume of goods which can be bought from the United States, and that on the other hand continued improvement in Canadian conditions brings corresponding increases in the volume of goods which they can sell us. From this viewpoint it might be considered economic statesmanship for the United States to discover means to increase their purchases from Canada rather than to consider measures which will constitute new trade barriers.
Any student of political economy will subscribe to the principle laid down by Sir Herbert Holt, and, paraphrasing his words, let me say: From this viewpoint it might be considered economic statesmanship for Canada to discover means to increase their purchases from Great Britain rather than to consider measures which will constitute new trade barriers. Sir Herbert Holt continues:
As a last resort, it may be necessary to meet this situation by direct tariff increases and by granting further preference to Great Britain and to most favoured nations.
When a known protectionist like Sir Herbert Holt advocates an increase in the British preference, one would not expect this government, which claims to be a low tariff government, to be putting further trade barriers in the way of Great Britain.
The following is a resolution passed at a recent convention of the United Farmers of Canada, held at Saskatoon:
Whereas the existence and continuation of agriculture in the prairie provinces depends upon satisfactory markets being found and maintained for wheat;
And whereas at the present time Great Britain buys a very high percentage of our wheat, while the United States virtually ex-eludes it by a prohibitive tariff;
And whereas Great Britain must sell her manufactured goods if she is going to be able to buy our agricultural products;
And whereas it is the avowed purpose of the Republican party to increase the duty against Canadian agricultural products;
And whereas many lines of goods now purchased from the United States could be supplied by the British manufacturers, Which could create a greater purchasing power for our wheat and other agricultural products;
Now therefore be it resolved that we call upon the government of Canada to immediately increase the British preference, and provide for successive reductions each year until we have free trade with Great Britain.
Let me appeal to the minister and particularly to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to implement the pledges and assurances which they gave to the house last year that this provision would not be allowed to do what we know it is doing at the present time. I trust that if the government cannot see its way clear to eliminate the regulation alto-
The. Budget-Mr. Cam-pbell

gether, it will at least modify it to eliminate those products that cannot be economically produced within the empire.
I have just a few moments left and I wish to refer briefly to a matter which was brought up in the house by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) when he spoke on the address. He drew the attention of the government to an agitation that was going on in western Canada asking for the dismissal of the Board of Grain Commissioners. I am not going to constitute myself a judge of the Board of Grain Commissioners, but this agitation cannot be overlooked; it cannot be dismissed because there is more behind it than a mere demagogic impulse. Resolutions were passed by the United Farmers of Alberta and the United Farmers of Canada calling for the dismissal of the board. I thought, after the matter was drawn to the attention of the government by the hon. member for Acadia, we would have had some pronouncement from the government, and I wish to point out now that we should have some pronouncement. This cannot be ignored and it cannot be delayed.
For some reason or another-I am not going to say just how-certain sections of the Canada Grain Act were ignored and overridden last year by grain companies. Sections 150 and 225 are the ones about which we have heard these complaints. Section 150 of the Canada Grain Act gives to the producer the right to determine the destination of his grain. We know that pool farmers placing their grain in line elevators have been refused that right time after time by private grain companies. Section 225 stipulates the form of ticket that shall be used, and it says that no ticket except that provided by statute or by an order in council shall be used. The ticket to which the hon. member for Acadia referred, and which is commonly called the "hybrid" ticket, was in general use last year. It is not one of those prescribed by statute; it is not covered by any order in council and yet, while repeated complaints were made to the Board of Grain Commissioners, no action whatever, so far as we know, was taken to carry out the law. As I say, we have no government pronouncement of policy with respect to the matter and we are entirely in the dark as to what the government propose to do. There are rumours-
I have read them in the press-that the government propose to ask parliament for a change in the Grain Act. It is absurd for the government to come and ask parliament for another change in the Grain Act until we enforce what we have at the present time. That
rMr. Campbell.]
is what the farmers are asking for to-day and until an honest attempt has been made to enforce the act, it is useless to come to the house and ask for other changes. I wish to impress this matter on the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) who, I am sorry, is not in his seat. So far he seems to be very sympathetic to suggestions that were made to him from this side of the house, but I want to point out to him that the temper of the western farmer is such that this cannot be ignored, and neither this government nor any other self-respecting body would want to have its statutes overridden as these have been. The fact that these two clauses in the Grain Act-have been overridden during the past year has cost our western pools some millions of dollars. Millions of bushels of grain that should have gone directly to the pool terminals went to the terminals of the line companies. We know what has happened there; the grain is mixed down to what we call the minimum of the grade. The cream of the grain is sold and the premium secured and the skim milk, as it were, is turned over to the pool. In addition to that there are serious complaints of alteration in routing. Many factors that I cannot explain at the present time enter into this, but I wish to impress upon the government that it is imperative that some action be taken at the earliest possible moment with respect to the matter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in company with other members, I take very keen pleasure in saying a few words in unqualified approval of the budget, so ably prepared and presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). Ordinarily, a budget, being composed almost entirely of figures, makes very dry and uninteresting reading; but in the present instance at the very outset vivid interest is aroused by the figures quoted, in view of the fact that they mean a substantial reduction in our net debt of 850,984,137.17 for the fiscal year 1927-28, and that the estimated total revenues for the fiscal year 1928-29, ending March 31, will be in the neighbourhood of $454,942,000. Nothing can speak more highly in favour of the present administration than these figures, and, w'hen the increases of $28000.000 in customs revenue, $6,000,000 in excise duties, $1,900,000 in income taxes, $660,000 interest on investments, and $840,000 from miscellaneous sources are taken into consideration, even the youngest student of statistics is struck by the results. A rapid calculation of revenue and expenditures gives the gratifying result of $69,782,000 of estimated surphn revenue.


The Budget-Mr. Perms
The scrupulously clear compilation of figures prepared by the hon. Minister of Finance shows that Canada's finances are in competent hands and that we need have no fear of mismanagement. Figures do not lie, and the substantial increase in revenue over expenditures can mean nothing but commendation of the government and its methods. No effort has been spared to place before the public, in a most implicit manner, undeniable proof of honest endeavour, combined with ability, to place Canada on an enviable footing. Progress is the watchword.
There is something in this year's budget to meet all requirements. The reduction in the sales tax will please the purchaser; the reduction in the national debt will please everybody ; improvements in various services have been carried out, and although there is bound to be some criticism-for if there were no criticism there would be no opposition-yet there is no denying that this government has done wonders.
It is indeed a very great honour, Mr. Speaker, of which I am deeply appreciative, to represent in this parliament the county of Wrighf. Situated as it is along that wonder-fid valley [DOT] of the Gatineau-and I may say in the heart of the Laurentian hills-it is unsurpassed in beauty and in picturesqueness by any portion of the so-much talked of and so much admired Swiss Alps. I doubt indeed if the grandeur of the Rockies can compare with the beauty of the Gatineau valley and the Laurentian hills. But, sir, I am not only concerned about the physical features of that wonderful country; but I am even more anxious to see that the interests of those pioneers be looked after as a component part of this great dominion. I am satisfied that those interests, diversified as they are, have been well safeguarded by the policy of the Liberal government, and particularly by the budget speech of the hon. the Minister of Finance.
Of course we all know that agriculture is at the base of the national prosperity of Canada, and that to that hard-working, self-sacrificing and patriotic class we owe a great deal. But I feel that by virtue of the Liberal policies those interests are well protected under the able administration of the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). I want to state clearly that this basic industry of agriculture must continue to be safeguarded, to be properly looked after, and that the interests of those who contribute such a large part to our national existence should continue to receive all the care and attention to which they are so well entitled.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is one subject on which I must say a few words-the Beau-harnois project, which loomed up not so very long ago as a mountain of contention and resolved itself into a national windfall. There . is no doubt whatever that the realization of this enterprise will mean a lasting benefit to Canada. The bugbear of a monopoly of untold magnitude has been duly enlarged upon, but this argument was met by such an able refutation that even those who wavered in their allegiance became firmly convinced of the necessity of supporting this measure.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), in laying before the house all the data in connection with this undertaking, left nothing to be guessed at; with the exception of the technical details that must necessarily be left to expert engineers, we know all there is to be known about this great national enterprise. The findings of the advisory board, the decisions arrived at in conference, and the wording of agreements have given us ample assurance that Canadian rights will be protected in every possible way and no serious-minded Canadian citizen can possibly feel alarmed because an undertaking of great magnitude has been consummated. There are, of course, conscientious objectors, but the really fair-minded, far-sighted business man could not but feel that he is in duty bound to give the project favourable consideration.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must say that one does not need to be an incurable optimist to feel elated over the success that has attended the efforts of this administration, and even the confirmed pessimist will eventu-aly, if he finds it too difficult to become a convert, silently fold his tent, and, like the Arabs, steal away. I do not want to pose as an extremist in fair weather prophecy, but the figures have been tabled, concrete results have been shown, and deficits are conspicuous by their absence-what better proof could' be asked for?
On motion of Mr. Brown, the debate was adj ourned.
On motion of Mr. Robb the house adjourned at 10.40 p.m.
